R.E.P.O is the kind of game that starts with “okay, let’s do one quick run” and ends with everyone screaming, laughing, and questioning their teamwork skills. It somehow turns simple objectives into absolute chaos in the best way possible. One moment you’re calmly trying to do your job, and the next you’re running for your life while your friends are making *very* unhelpful decisions.

What really makes R.E.P.O shine is how naturally funny it is. The physics, timing, and unexpected disasters feel perfectly designed to create comedy without trying too hard. You don’t even need to be good at the game to have fun—in fact, being bad might make it even better. Every failed attempt feels like a story worth retelling.

The atmosphere is tense enough to keep you on edge, but never so serious that it stops being fun. It balances suspense and humor perfectly, turning panic into laughter almost instantly. And when you play with friends, the game becomes a nonstop highlight reel of mistakes, heroic sacrifices, and blaming each other for everything that goes wrong.

Overall, R.E.P.O is pure fun. It’s goofy, stressful, unpredictable, and endlessly entertaining. If you enjoy games that create unforgettable moments, inside jokes, and lots of laughing (and yelling), R.E.P.O is absolutely worth playing.

a piano that weighs approximately the same as the moon
a friend who dropped a priceless ceramic vase down the stairs immediately

and a cart we lost in the first two minutes and never spoke of again.
The objective is simple. Carry valuable items carefully to extraction. Do not break them. We have never once done this.
The physics system is a masterpiece of human suffering:
"Okay, careful, careful—"
The vase flies sideways into a wall.
It was worth $4,000.

The proximity voice chat adds incredible immersion. You can hear your friends whispering in real time as you creep through a dark mansion. The upgrade shop offers meaningful progression. We bought better lungs. We needed better lungs because we keep screaming. We are still screaming. We just have more health while we do it.

Probably the only "lethal company-like" (or whatever you wanna call it) that I like, including the original Lethal Company. While Lethal Company is still a good game and commendable for popularizing the gameplay loop it has, it's still primarily a game where you're meant to die in various ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ways for laughs. REPO still expects you to die eventually, but the tools you have are way stronger, and how you play the game can vary a lot on the gear you buy and the party you have. Early game REPO is more faithful to the original genre since you have very little gear, but once you get your first weapons the game really sets itself apart. You can absolutely play the game like a horror game and run away/hide from every enemy, but you can also play the game like it's DOOM and go around trying to kill every monster on the map. Weapons aside, there's a lot of very useful equipment that feels good to use. The point being is that the REPO devs do a great job of making the gameplay itself fun and engaging, instead of it essentially being a way to kill the player and make your friends laugh. Also, unlike plenty of other games in the genre this game gets consistent, and quality, updates. I can't think of a single update since launch that I thought was bad.

review:
[h1]Don't drop that![/h1]
I've played R.E.P.O. for several hours now and I'm thoroughly impressed! The game delivers on all fronts. The cooperative experience with up to six players creates the perfect mix of tension, horror, and chaos. The core idea works brilliantly: salvage valuable items and transport them to safety while creepy creatures hunt you down. It's called "Retrieve, Extract and Profit Operation" for a reason you're constantly on the move, always under pressure. And that's exactly what makes it so much fun.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
R.E.P.O.'s gameplay blends co-op teamwork, strategic planning, and nerve-wracking tension. As part of a salvage crew, you and up to five other players enter abandoned industrial facilities, research complexes, or run-down residential areas. Your mission: find valuable objects, salvage them, and bring them safely to the extraction zone, all while maximizing profit.

What sounds simple quickly becomes an intense balancing act. Every item has weight and physical properties. A TV rattles, a piano is to heavy to carry, and a dropped object can make enough noise to alert the creatures to your presence. They react to sounds and movements, so caution and coordination are everything.

The proximity voice chat creates an authentic atmosphere: you only hear each other when standing close together. This leads to realistic, often chaotic moments, like when someone disappears into the darkness with a valuable object and frantically calls for help. Every mission becomes a mix of horror, tactics, and pure adrenaline.

[h1]Development[/h1]
A major plus for R.E.P.O. is the active and dedicated development. The small studio semiwork clearly cares about the community: updates arrive regularly, and feedback from Steam forums or Discord is quickly addressed. The team listens closely and responds to player requests, whether for balancing, difficulty adjustments, or physics fine-tuning.

[h1]Final words[/h1]
R.E.P.O. is an exciting, atmospheric co-op horror experience that excels with clever gameplay, physics-based challenges, and unpredictable monsters. The engine delivers realistic interactions and a dense atmosphere, while an active community continuously improves the game. Anyone who loves teamplay, thrills, and tactical horror will find a real gem here, remarkably polished even in Early Access. 

Cheers.

I do really like this game, but it desperately needs some balancing adjustments, especially early-game in the first few maps and in single-player mode. As it currently exists, I have a very love-but-mostly-hate relationship with it.

The game is fine in multiplayer mode. It's silly, it's fun with your friends, and its mechanics aren't difficult to pick up and learn. However, it is JUST fine. The monsters need to be balanced much better than they are, ESPECIALLY some of the tier 3 monsters and ESPECIALLY for the first 1~4 levels of the game. You shouldn't be contending with a tier 3 headman monster in the first or second map of a new game when you've still got no tools, weapons, or meaningful upgrades to help you deal with it. Tier 3 monsters should not be spawning in the first couple levels of the game at all in their current state when they can be so abysmally difficult to deal with.

If the devs don't want to touch any of that, then there should at least be vanilla tools that let you customize the game spawns or overall difficulty to your preference. It's not fun playing in a group of 5 where the same 1-2 players are the only ones left alive on every level because your more casual or weaker or simply misfortunate friends continuously just get totally annihilated by the floating head or a clown. Yes, I'm complaining directly from personal experience because it surely cannot be fun having our friends watching me and my one other friend have to struggle through each and every map by ourselves whilst trying to return our friends' heads to each extraction point because we just can't keep them alive against tier 2 and 3 monsters. This is supposed to be a fun and silly friend "party" game, not a sweaty GET GUD BRO game. Let us please make it more enjoyable for our friend groups to play.

Finally, all of these complains extend into the single-player mode. In single player on the very first map, I should NOT have to be dealing with a headman and a bowtie with my vanilla butt with no upgrades, weapons, or tools to assist me while ALSO having no one else there to help kite the monster away or keep going if I die. That's just senseless. The single-player is far too annoying to bother with, and I feel like tweaking it to either incorporate more balance with the monsters or allowing more stable scaled progression would help tremendously.

TLDR; I love the game but its lack of balance, difficulty scaling, and customization is extremely frustrating. After who-knows-how-many levels (perhaps there could be a set goal in the settings?), the players could emerge onto that platform, not as losers, but as winners. They can sip tea (like eating a consumable), then take out their angst for certain monsters by placing toy-sized versions of them on an extraction table that smashes them. All of the while, credits can roll. And here’s another fun aspect to the idea. If they want, they can allow their teamwork to shine and all become REPO winners, or they can take each other out as with the other ending and become “king of the winners”. It could be an even better tag than losing because they reached a goal. So satisfying if you ask me. 

Reasons I think many people would enjoy an ending similar to this outline:
I love setting a goal and reaching it. I love smashing and venting frustration on the actual monsters (hence the smashing of those silly things in an after-party). I like the idea of a celebration tea, whether it be a teacup, cake, oil can, whatever the lore would suggest. I do like REPO, but there are so many frustrating things in this game that have ruined me enjoying this game as much as I'd want to enjoy it. There IS a good game here, but I don't see many people pointing out the MANY negative or frustrating aspects of this game, so I wanted to point some of these out and I hope the developers see this so the game can be the best that it can be.

Firstly let me talk about maybe my biggest issue, the Huntsman AI. I don't know why many people think he is ok, but I've heard it's worse on the host's end and I host often so maybe that's why I have such an Issue with it and others don't. I have had MANY times where he shoots me either across an entire room where I could not hope to react and get one tapped, or he shoots me when ANOTHER sound source made him trigger and he shoots me anyway. I've had times where I tap a object on the ground to bait his shot, and instead of shooting the object far away from me he shoots me instead. This makes absolutely no sense and I personally think he should not work this way, he should always shoot the sound source not the nearest player like how he does at times. I suggest taking inspiration from the Eyeless Dogs from Lethal Company, just make him not instantly shoot at the first sound he hears and make him have an audio cue where players can be aware they are making too much noise like a sound of him grumbling or him going "huh", and if they continue he then shoots them. I also think his idle sounds should play more often and have more range so you can hear him before you get in his range so less unfair deaths where you didn't even know he was there at the edge of your vision occur. I think in general the monsters in this game are too quiet/don't have idle sounds that are good sound cues. Besides some exceptions like the Loom/Robe, them being quiet is part of their design.

This is a little less important but, WHY DO SOME COSMETICS GIVE YOU ONE OUT OF A PAIR?! I genuinely don't understand why they did this, because I've had so many times where I get a cosmetic that looks like I'd use it... IF ONLY I GOT THE PAIR AND NOT ONE FOR A SINGLE SHOE/LEG. Some cosmetics do look cool asymmetrically, but (in my opinion) most don't and this just makes cosmetics grindy for the ones you want because the chances of getting the other one in the pair are low. I just don't see any positives to it being this way because if you wanted to just use one, you could just equip one out of the two if you got the cosmetic in a pair anyway. But I do like everything else about the cosmetic system they did a good job on how they work in every other way. I just really disagree with it working like this with pairs of cosmetics.

Back to another big issue (again in my opinion). The physics system is WAY to janky in some areas, mostly with big items. Big items take damage for absolutely no reason very often. Sometimes you'll just touch it to check the value... BOOM -$2,377 for no reason. Sometimes you'll slide it across the ground gently... BOOM -$5,078 for no reason. Sometimes you rotate it slightly... BOOM -$3,980 for no reason. The big items really need to be less janky because a lot of the time they quickly become not worth it because it randomly took damage from sliding on a carpeted floor. When moving big items is a main game mechanic, it should be polished.
 Also I'm not sure whether to call this a physics issue or not but, you also should not be able to hit yourself with a melee weapon so easily. Many times I've needed a melee weapon quickly and hit myself while pulling it out, getting me killed. 

I also have an issue with the early levels having a tier 3 enemy like a Trudge or Head, which would not be an issue if the levels had more paths. What often happens (especially when I played solo with the Trudge) is the monster blocks and camps where you need to go and they waste your time, and because its early game (especially bad on the first level) you can't deal with these guys and just have to wait 4-8min just for them to leave. I think this is worse with the Trudge because he is so slow and takes forever to leave and it's difficult to run past him without getting one shot. In the later levels this is not as bad because you and the monsters have more paths to go, but in early game it really can be frustrating and slow down the game more than it should. I would just make the early levels have more pathways to counter this issue. Also because I'm talking about the Trudge, I think he should not be able to kill you through walls and suck you in through walls either. But this could be a bug and not an intentional gameplay mechanic. I've also been killed by the Cleanup Crew (UH OH guy) when I was enclosed in a safe through the wall from the head explosion.

Another thing is the weapon spread from some ranged weapons (mostly the handgun and similar weapons). Some weapons have insane bullet spread (even after they buffed it). They already have limited ammo, why do I have to be in hugging distance to make sure I don't miss? It makes the weapons feel a tad underpowered.
 
The stamina system early game is a pain to deal with as well, mostly the recovery rate. The amount of stamina you get early game is barely enough to survive and if you aren't in a good spot, don't have full stamina or don't hide perfectly; you just die to some enemies without a chance(head, duck, Robe etc.). You can upgrade both of these aspects, but in a game where you're playing with multiple people you don't get enough till very late because everyone needs it. I think they should AT LEAST make stamina recovery faster with no upgrades.

But that's all. I do enjoy this game, but I don't see people talking about these issues, (even though some can be seen as nitpicks) some can kill the fun of the game (Huntsman). It's ok to criticize a game, it can still be good. It helps the game be the best it can be. For anyone who read this, thank you for reading my rant/critique. I hope the developers take this feedback because there is a really good game here held back by some frustration, and unfair AI, mechanics or bugs.
Thank you for reading!

“Friendslop” is a term that has been becoming increasingly popular lately, and I feel like it diminishes something very valuable: a game that makes you laugh with your friends. A game like R.E.P.O.

In R.E.P.O., we have to collect a series of objects, fit them into a small, limited-space cart, bring them back to the base, and sell them for enough money to advance to the next level. The more objects we put in the cart, the less space we have, and questions start to arise: Will this object fit? Could I make it work if I rearrange everything? Will I be able to move the cart without everything falling out?

Now add the fact that every object has its own size, shape, durability, weight, and behavior. And, to add even more tension, there are monsters capable not only of killing us, but also of destroying what we are carrying in the cart. Each one has its own unique way of interacting with us and our environment.

As we progress through the game and heavier objects start appearing, we are (almsot always) forced to work with someone else to carry them and figure out how to get them back to the base. It is similar to moving houses, where a couple of people have to figure out how to carry and fit some enormous piece of furniture through a tiny doorway. Except here, you cannot just sit down and think about it or stand still for too long, because you might get hit with a jumpscare that makes you drop the object, break it, or simply die.

With all these variables, it is no surprise that R.E.P.O. has become the clip-generating machine that it was—and still is. But these moments are not simply the result of putting realistic physics into a game and waiting for something funny to happen. They are the result of good design.

And even its premise fits into this. The “story” is basically about a greedy tax collector who sends us out to repossess things, while we carry out the job as the result of an “apparent debt.” It is about greed and ambition.

And believe me: many times you will find yourself wondering whether what you are carrying in that cart is really worth it. Whether it is worth risking everything for one more valuable object, even when you already have enough to finish the level.

(Spoiler: greed comes at a cost.)

R.E.P.O. is not particularly visually creative, it does not have a deep or terrifying story, and it does not even have an ending. . And it does not need any of that to convey a feeling. All it needs is its own language: physics, order, and strategy in an arcade game, with money essentially functioning as the score.

The language of video games.

[b]I decided to check out R.E.P.O. because, well, everyone and their grandma was posting about it. You know how it goes: trending everywhere, gotta see what the fuss is about. And yeah, it’s got flashes of “this could be fun,” but also enough quirks to make you raise an eyebrow (or ten).

What grabbed me first was how fast-paced and chaotic things get. There’s an energy to the matches that feels raw: weapons fire, grenades fly, and decisions are split-second. When things go right, you and your squad breaching a room, nails hitting the wall, hearts pounding, enemies dropping, there’s a real sense of "we did it, lads." It’s the kind of rush that makes you remember why shooters can be so addictive.

But here’s where R.E.P.O. stumbles: sometimes the chaos is too chaotic. Guns feel inconsistent; a spray-and-pray might work once and flop the next time. Match balance can swing wildly, one moment you’re dominating, the next you’re getting fragged by someone who moves like they’ve got a jetpack. The learning curve and randomness make it tough to feel like skill is always rewarded. On top of that, a few bugs and lag spikes popped up during my sessions, nothing catastrophic, but enough to remind me that this game is still a bit rough around the edges.

All jokes aside, R.E.P.O. is a “love-it-or-leave-it” type game. For a casual go-at-it-with-friends shoot-em-up, it’s got some fun in it. Just don’t go in expecting the most polished shooter out there, treat it more like a wobbly roller-coaster: exciting, unpredictable, and maybe a little nauseating after a while. If you’ve got time to spare and tolerance for mayhem, give it a shot. But if you're picky about balance and consistency, maybe hold the trigger finger.[/b]

If you're looking for a co-op horror game that delivers pure chaos, tension, and nonstop laughter, then R.E.P.O. is an absolute must-play. This game perfectly balances horror and comedy in a way that feels fresh and incredibly addictive. Every session turns into an unforgettable experience where teamwork, panic, and stupidity collide in the best possible way.

The physics-based gameplay is what truly makes the game shine. Carrying valuable objects carefully while terrifying monsters hunt your team creates constant tension, but somehow the funniest moments happen when everything goes horribly wrong. One second you're silently coordinating with friends, and the next someone accidentally destroys the loot, slams a door into another teammate, or screams while running for their life. It never gets old.

The atmosphere is also surprisingly immersive. Dark environments, unsettling sound design, and unpredictable enemy encounters keep you constantly on edge. Even after several matches, the game still manages to create genuine fear and adrenaline. At the same time, the proximity voice chat makes every moment feel natural and hilarious, especially during panic situations.

What makes R.E.P.O stand out from many other co-op horror games is how replayable it feels. No match ever plays out the same way, and the randomness of player behavior creates endless entertainment. Whether you’re playing seriously or just messing around with friends, the game is ridiculously fun.

Overall, R.E.P.O is one of the best multiplayer horror experiences in recent years. Funny, stressful, chaotic, and incredibly memorable. If you enjoy co-op games with friends, this is easily worth your time.

REPO has been some of the most fun I’ve had in co-op gaming in a long time. My friends and I dumped endless hours into it, along with several years off our lives from stress, laughter, and complete nonsense. Most of the tears were from laughing so hard we could barely function. The rest were from those moments where everything goes catastrophically wrong, the run implodes, and you are kicked all the way back to the beginning, which is the exact point where you start considering whether gaming is really your hobby or if maybe it’s time to take up knitting.

That is the magic of REPO. It is absolute chaos. Beautiful, stupid, panic-filled chaos. One second your group is locked in, focused, and working like a machine. The next second one bad move turns into a full collapse, everybody is screaming, someone is dead, someone else is blaming the wrong person, and somehow it is the funniest thing you have ever seen.

Even in a small group, this game was incredible. But once we added a few mods, it really became dangerous. Health boost, store expansion, buff sharing, all great. But the true gift from the heavens was the LEVEL SAVE. That mod deserves a shrine. Once we could save progress on a level instead of getting launched back to level 1 every time the game decided to beat us with a chair, that is when the real fun began. Suddenly the suffering had structure. The pain had purpose.

And that is the thing, REPO somehow turns failure into bonding. Through the jump scares, the laughter, the yelling, the tears, and the absolute nonsense, I genuinely bonded with people through this game. Few games can say that. It is frustrating in the exact right ways, hilarious in ways you cannot plan for, and unforgettable with the right group.

Hats off to the devs. REPO is chaos, comedy, suffering, friendship, and questionable decision-making wrapped into one beautiful package. Easy 5/5.

Welcome to Repo, the only game where beating a child with a bat is not only morally acceptable but also financially profitable. There's no plot, and no desire to find one. Instead, there's chaos, monsters, strange companions, and a complete lack of the concept of "normal." In short, it's another drug addict simulator, like in Lethal Company—you're ripping out everything, both bolted and unbolted, from the house for a fix.
The atmosphere is like a crazy old man's house everything breaks, everyone's screaming, constant self-talk, someone's forgotten how to play again, the feeling that the map has a life of its own, and no one controls what's happening, and it all ends with you dragging all your companions because, well, someone has to. Here, every other moment feels like a scene from a dream with a temperature of 39°C you roll under a table while your partners are killing gnomes with screaming soundpads, and the guy with a gun in the corner is taking out everyone with a Nouscope 180, including you, because he's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ awesome. The truth of life is this: a crowd can take out even a blind guy with a gun. A separate art form—your partner's face after an encounter with some evil spirit—is truly the most devastating (literally) thing you'll see while sitting in silence at the blind guy's feet. You can also destroy a store with just a rubber ducky, or buy a bat and the monsters will run away screaming. With each new level, your moral compass decreases. The less shame you feel, the better your experience will be. And despite all this chaos, you feel like you're actually doing something useful. Even if you're just carrying your fallen partner's head through this madhouse, even if you've been lying under the table the entire game, that counts as a contribution here.
And remember: don't trust the cute ducks and stay away from the crazy Wolverine woman on the minimum settings with your cart. Even if you die, it's no big deal. They'll find you, report you, resurrect you, and throw you back into hell.
